analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on petroleum and corporations to fund toxic waste site cleanup through 2018.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, so the polluter-funded taxes that expired in 1995 stayed expired.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. Its dedicated funding taxes — a per-barrel tax on petroleum and a corporate environmental income tax — were allowed to lapse at the end of 1995, shifting cleanup costs from polluting industries onto general tax revenues. This bill would have brought those taxes back through the end of 2017, restoring the 'polluter pays' funding stream. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents living near hazardous waste sites, who would benefit from faster and better-funded cleanups, and taxpayers generally, who would no longer bear the full cost of Superfund cleanup out of general revenues. Chemical and petroleum companies that create the hazardous substances covered by the tax would pay it instead.

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate — an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products — and the corporate environmental income tax, both of which had applied only through 1995, and extends them through the end of 2017. [S2] [S3]

Reinstating these taxes would refill the dedicated Superfund trust fund, restoring the 'polluter pays' principle under which the industries whose products create hazardous waste help finance cleanup rather than general taxpayers alone. [S3]
The bill also makes a technical change to remove export provisions from the excise tax, so exported crude is treated consistently with domestic petroleum. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Petroleum refiners, importers, and petrochemical companies, who pay the excise tax and the corporate environmental income tax, and ultimately their customers to the extent the taxes are passed through in prices.

drawbacks.text: The taxes would be passed through to consumers in the prices of gasoline and petroleum-based products, raising energy costs somewhat for ordinary households. [S3]

The Superfund program's cleanup record and cost-effectiveness have long been criticized, so refilling its trust fund does not guarantee faster or better cleanups; the bill adds no program reforms, only money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is restoring a dedicated funding stream for cleaning up toxic sites under the polluter-pays principle, instead of leaving cleanup costs to general taxpayers. The cost is a modest price increase in petroleum products and higher corporate taxes. The bill's weakness is that it funds the program as-is without addressing long-standing criticisms of Superfund's pace and administration, but its core tradeoff — industry pays versus everyone pays — favors the polluter-pays approach.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in September 2007, never got a hearing, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on September 24, 2007, joined by Rep. Frank Pallone, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation. [S1] [S3] [S5]
Sixteen House members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill. [S4]
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired at the end of the 110th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum and chemical companies are better off: the polluter-funded Superfund taxes stayed expired, and cleanup costs continued to fall on general taxpayers. Communities near toxic sites gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the Superfund financing taxes. [S1] [S3]

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction. [S3]

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on September 24, 2007 and never held a hearing or markup on it. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsors appear in the record, and the tax-writing committee never took it up. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would reimpose the per-barrel Superfund excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products that lapsed at the end of 1995, a direct cost the industry avoided for over a decade. Reinstatement would shift a share of toxic-site cleanup funding back onto the industry.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and other large corporations
industries.note: The corporate environmental income tax on corporations' alternative minimum taxable income, an additional 0.12 percent, would return through 2017. These companies have benefited from the tax's expiration since the Superfund trust fund's dedicated revenues ran out and general taxpayers took over cleanup funding.
A refilled Superfund trust fund would support more funded cleanup projects, meaning more contracted work. Their interest tracks the public's interest in completed cleanups.
